criteria: Published by a recognized news organization or official public agency
Connected to at least one Family PD pillar
Offers a practical prevention, preparation, or family-learning opportunity

stories.title: Charlotte leaders call for deeper community involvement to prevent teen violence
stories.summary: After multiple deadly shootings involving teenagers, Charlotte police and community leaders emphasized de-escalation, responsibility, education, mentoring, and sustained adult involvement. The report highlights that prevention requires families, mentors, schools, community programs, and volunteers working together.
prevention: Talk with children and teens about conflict, online arguments, social-media bullying, and de-escalation before a crisis occurs.
Identify trusted adults, mentors, programs, and safe places young people can use when emotions or conflict escalate.
Practice a family plan for walking away, contacting an adult, reporting threats, and getting emergency help.
Support or volunteer with credible youth-development and violence-prevention organizations in the community.
stories.prompts: Who can each young person in our family contact when conflict feels unsafe? What online or in-person situations require walking away and getting adult help? Which community program, mentor, coach, faith leader, or volunteer opportunity could strengthen our support network?

stories.title: Federal investment expands Registered Apprenticeship opportunities
stories.summary: The U.S. Department of Labor announced $162 million to expand Registered Apprenticeship in key industries, creating more earn-while-you-learn career opportunities.
prevention: Compare apprenticeship, college, CTE, certification, and workforce-program options before choosing a pathway.
Ask whether a program is registered, paid, connected to employers, and clear about credentials earned.
Include transportation, work schedules, childcare, equipment, and long-term wages in the family decision.
Use official apprenticeship and workforce sources rather than relying only on advertisements.
stories.prompts: Which family members could benefit from paid training? What career fields match their interests? What questions should we ask before enrolling in a program?

stories.title: Sudden severe storm turns a holiday boat trip into a tragedy
stories.summary: A sudden severe storm overwhelmed a recreational boat on Geneva Lake. Three children died even though the children were wearing life jackets, showing how quickly weather conditions can exceed a family’s ability to react.
prevention: Check forecasts and active alerts immediately before outdoor or water activities.
Decide in advance which weather conditions mean the activity stops or the family returns to shore.
Use life jackets, but do not treat safety equipment as a replacement for weather decisions and evacuation timing.
Create a communication and reunification plan for outings.
stories.prompts: What warning signs or weather alerts would make our family cancel or leave an activity? Who checks the forecast? What is our emergency communication and meeting plan during an outing?

stories.title: Making a family plan for summer screen time
stories.summary: The FTC encouraged families to discuss online rules and expectations and consider parental controls for content, time limits, communication, purchases, location sharing, and separate device profiles.
prevention: Agree on screen-time expectations before conflict occurs.
Review who children can communicate with through games and social platforms.
Use device profiles, passcodes, privacy settings, and age-appropriate parental controls.
Discuss how online activity affects sleep, mood, school, safety, and family relationships.
stories.prompts: What are our current screen-time expectations? Which apps, games, chats, purchases, or location settings need review? What should children do when an unknown person contacts them?

stories.title: Education and HHS launch new family-engagement and school-support grants
stories.summary: New federal grant competitions emphasize literacy, tutoring, family engagement, and community partnerships that support students.
prevention: Ask schools what tutoring, literacy, mentoring, and family-engagement supports are available.
Use school and district websites, newsletters, portals, and family events to find programs early.
Keep a simple list of contacts for teachers, counselors, family-engagement staff, and community partners.
Discuss which supports match the student’s actual need rather than waiting for a crisis.
stories.prompts: Which school supports do we know how to access? Who is our main school contact? What service or partnership could help our family now?

stories.title: What families should know after the Canvas cyberattack
stories.summary: The FTC warned that after a school technology breach, scammers may impersonate schools or companies. Families were advised not to trust links or contact information in unexpected messages and to use known school or company channels.
prevention: Do not click links or call numbers in unexpected breach-related messages.
Contact the school or company through a known website, phone number, or email address.
Review account passwords and use multifactor authentication where available.
Know where to find identity-theft and data-breach guidance before it is needed.
stories.prompts: How would we verify a message claiming our school account or personal information was exposed? Which family accounts need stronger passwords or multifactor authentication? Who should children ask before responding?

stories.title: That unexpected job-offer text is probably a scam
stories.summary: The FTC reported fake recruiters sending generic texts about remote jobs, then asking people to send money, deposit fake checks, or put personal money into online tasks.
prevention: Do not engage with generic, unexpected job texts or messaging-app offers.
Never pay money to get paid or secure a job.
Verify employers through the organization’s official website and published contact information.
Ask a trusted adult or experienced job seeker to review unfamiliar offers.
stories.prompts: What signs make a job offer suspicious? How will our family verify recruiters and employers? What information or money should never be provided during an unexpected job conversation?

stories.title: Labor Department launches tools for AI skills in apprenticeships
stories.summary: A new federal resource helps apprenticeship programs integrate artificial intelligence skills and industry-specific training into career pathways.
prevention: Treat AI literacy as a career skill while continuing to build reading, math, communication, and technical foundations.
Verify what an AI training program teaches and whether employers recognize the resulting skills.
Practice using AI as an assistant while checking accuracy and protecting private information.
Build a portfolio that shows real work rather than relying only on course completion.
stories.prompts: Where is AI already changing work our family is interested in? Which foundational skills still matter? What could we build or practice to demonstrate learning?

stories.title: FTC explains how common scams begin on social media
stories.summary: The FTC warned that social-media scams often use fake sales, investment offers, impersonation, and urgent messages to steal money or personal information.
prevention: Pause before sending money, sharing codes, or clicking links from social-media messages.
Verify people and companies using contact information found independently.
Search the name of an offer or company with words such as scam or complaint.
Report suspicious accounts and discuss scams openly so embarrassment does not prevent someone from asking for help.
stories.prompts: Which scams are most likely to reach our family? What is our rule for sending money or verification codes? Who should we ask before acting on an urgent message?

stories.title: FAFSA completion grows as families gain updated college outcome information
stories.summary: The Department of Education reported more than 10 million processed 2026–27 FAFSA forms and updated College Scorecard information on post-graduation earnings.
prevention: Complete financial-aid forms early and save copies of confirmation information.
Compare total cost, grants, loans, graduation rates, credentials, and likely earnings—not just the school name.
Review aid offers carefully and ask what must be repaid.
Discuss affordable alternatives such as community college, CTE, apprenticeships, and employer-paid education.
stories.prompts: What does our family need to learn about FAFSA and financial aid? How will we compare program cost with likely outcomes? Which lower-cost pathways should remain on the table?

stories.title: New federal resources focus on student attendance and engagement
stories.summary: Federal guidance highlights the many reasons students miss school, including health, caregiving, work, transportation, and disengagement, and points families and schools toward supportive responses.
prevention: Track absences and patterns before they become a larger academic problem.
Ask what barrier is behind the absence instead of assuming a motivation problem.
Contact the school early about health, transportation, bullying, caregiving, disability, or work-related barriers.
Create a morning, transportation, and backup communication plan.
stories.prompts: What usually causes absences or lateness in our household? Who should we contact at school? What backup plan would make attendance easier?

stories.title: CDC campaign connects youth substance use and mental health conversations
stories.source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
stories.summary: CDC launched the Free Mind campaign with resources for youth ages 12–17 and caregivers about substance use, mental health, and how the two can affect each other.
prevention: Create regular, nonjudgmental opportunities for young people to talk about stress, substances, and peer pressure.
Know warning signs and identify trusted adults and professional supports before a crisis.
Discuss how sleep, social media, relationships, trauma, and substances can affect mood and decisions.
Avoid shame-based reactions that make children hide problems.
stories.prompts: Which adults can our children talk to without fear? What warning signs would concern us? How can we make difficult conversations feel safer?
